# Results — Study 923 (The Cash Lag) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Two questions, stamped
separately. **A — the measurement:** how fast does each cash vehicle pass the 13-week
bill rate (**^IRX**) through into its own realised return? **B — the trade:** does the
direction of rates tell you which vehicle to hold? Rule: the sign of the trailing 21-day
change in ^IRX through day **t**, acted on at **t+1** (the study's only execution lag) —
rates rising → hold **USFR** (zero-duration floating-rate notes), rates falling → hold
**SHV** (the longest cash ladder). Long-only, so no shorting and no borrow cost; 2 bps
one-way per leg (a switch trades two legs) charged on NAV. Every arm is measured
**excess-of-cash**, where cash is **BIL**'s own total return. Daily total-return closes
(`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`); ^IRX is a **yield quote**, not a total return. As-of
**2026-06-30** (the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| BIL, USFR, SHV + ^IRX | 2014-02-04 → 2026-06-30 | 3,118 | Fingerprint `d78f3661ba09` |

USFR's 2014 inception gates the headline window. **SGOV** (inception 2020-05) joins as a
fourth-vehicle cross-check on its own 2020-06-01 → 2026-06-30 window (n = 1,528). The
window covers the 2015-18 hiking cycle, the 2020 zero floor, the 2022-23 spike from 0% to
5.4% and the 2024-26 cuts — the largest short-rate cycle in forty years.

**Survivorship.** These are the four *surviving*, large, liquid cash ETFs. Two of them
(SGOV, USFR) are young and were launched into a world that had already selected for
cheap-and-short; funds that were mis-designed for the 2022 hiking cycle are not on this
tape. The dispersion measured below is therefore an *upper* bound on what a 2014 investor
could have picked between, not a lower one.

---

# A. The measurement — the lag is real, and it orders exactly as bond maths says

## A1. Realised effective duration (window-free)

Daily total return regressed on the daily change in ^IRX; the slope × (−100) is the
vehicle's realised duration in years. No trailing window is involved, so this number
carries **no averaging artefact** — it is the cleanest measurement in the study.

| Vehicle | What it holds | Nominal WAM | Realised duration | HAC *t* | n |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **USFR** | floating-rate Treasury notes (weekly coupon reset) | 5 d | **−0.001 yr** | −0.04 | 3,117 |
| **SGOV** | 0-3 month T-bills | 25 d | **+0.072 yr** | **+5.79** | 1,527 |
| **BIL** | 1-3 month T-bills | 45 d | **+0.083 yr** | **+7.57** | 3,117 |
| **SHV** | 0-1 year Treasuries | 110 d | **+0.177 yr** | **+8.05** | 3,117 |

The ordering is exactly the published-WAM ordering, and every non-zero duration clears
|*t*| = 5.8. USFR's duration is a **precise zero** — a floating-rate note whose coupon
resets weekly genuinely takes no mark-to-market hit when rates move. The nominal WAMs are
a **PROXY/ASSUMPTION** (issuer fund pages, current values) used only to state the a-priori
ordering; nothing in the calculation uses them.

**Units, named.** The slope is taken against **^IRX, a *discount*-yield quote**, not a
bond-equivalent yield. A bond-equivalent conversion would scale every duration in the column
by roughly +3%, which moves no ordering and no conclusion — but the numbers above are
"years of duration per point of *discount* quote", and that is what they should be read as.

## A2. Distributed-lag pass-through of ^IRX into the realised-yield proxy

The realised-yield proxy is a **labelled PROXY**: the vehicle's own trailing 21-day total
return, annualised, in percent — *not* an SEC 30-day yield or a book yield. It contains
both the carry the fund earns and the mark-to-market a rate move inflicts, which is what
the holder actually lives through. Below: the 21-day change in that proxy regressed on the
21-day change in ^IRX at lags 0, 7, … 63 days, HAC (42 lags).

| Vehicle | Σβ (eventual pass-through) | β at lag 0 (the duration shock) | *t* | Peak lag | Centroid lag |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SGOV | +0.98 | **−0.80** | −2.88 | 35 d | 26.7 d |
| BIL | +0.98 | **−1.16** | **−9.99** | 21 d | 23.1 d |
| USFR | +0.90 | +0.27 | +0.18 | 56 d | 40.4 d |
| SHV | +1.16 | **−3.26** | **−6.18** | 21 d | 22.7 d |

Two things fall straight out. **The coefficients sum to ~1** for every vehicle: a bill
portfolio eventually inherits the whole bill rate — full pass-through, no leakage.
**The lag-0 coefficient is the duration shock**, and it scales with WAM exactly as A1 says
(SHV −3.26, BIL −1.16, SGOV −0.80, USFR statistically zero). USFR's entire profile is
statistically empty — no significant coefficient anywhere — which is the correct reading
for an instrument with no lag and no duration: its 21-day realised return is dominated by
discount-margin wobble, not by where the bill rate was a month ago.

## A3. How much of the "lag" is the ruler? (proxy-window sweep)

A trailing *w*-day return mechanically averages the rate over *w* days, so part of any
measured lag is the measuring instrument. Re-running the centroid at four windows:

| Proxy window | SGOV | BIL | USFR | SHV |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 d | 16.1 | 18.7 | 32.7 | 12.7 |
| 10 d | 25.0 | 19.6 | 33.0 | 14.3 |
| 21 d | 26.7 | 23.1 | 40.4 | 22.7 |
| 42 d | 35.4 | 34.8 | 29.4 | 37.9 |

The centroid does drift upward with the window — so the honest headline is **not** "a
27-day lag". But at a 5-day window the centroid is still **13-19 days** for the three
bill funds, two to four times the ruler. There is a genuine repricing delay of roughly
**two to four weeks** underneath the artefact, and it is smaller than the naive 21-day
reading suggests. (USFR's centroid is meaningless: its coefficients are noise.)

## A4. Is the *measurement* era-robust? (the half that carries the stamp)

The trade gets an era cut in B5; the measurement has to face the same test, because it is
the half the Signal stamp rests on. Same split, same window-free regression:

| Era | n | USFR | BIL | SHV |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2014-2019 | 1,487 | +0.039 (*t* = +0.32) | +0.067 (*t* = **+2.82**) | +0.161 (*t* = **+6.64**) |
| 2020-2026 | 1,631 | −0.011 (*t* = −0.44) | +0.089 (*t* = **+7.59**) | +0.183 (*t* = **+7.19**) |

The ordering USFR < BIL < SHV holds in **both** halves, both bill funds clear |*t*| = 2.8 in
both, and USFR is a statistical zero in both. Unlike the trade, the measurement does not
depend on which rate cycle you look at — which is exactly what you expect from something
that is arithmetic rather than a forecast.

# B. The trade — nothing there, gross, and expensively negative net

## B1. The switch rule and its controls (21-day lookback, 2 bps one-way)

All excess of BIL's total return. `exSharpe` is the Sharpe *of the excess series*; on
cash-versus-cash differences the denominator is tens of basis points, so it is reported for
completeness and never leaned on — the annualised excess in bp and its HAC *t* are the
honest units here.

| Arm | Excess vs BIL | HAC *t* | exSharpe | Excess vol |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Switch rule (gross, 0 bps)** | **−6.9 bp/yr** | **−0.29** | −0.06 | 118 bp |
| Switch rule (net, 2 bps) | −115.3 bp/yr | −4.39 | −0.96 | 121 bp |
| Placebo — turnover-matched random switch (net) | −104.0 bp/yr | −4.70 | −0.94 | 110 bp |
| Placebo — the *reversed* rule (net) | −78.8 bp/yr | −3.51 | −0.85 | 93 bp |
| Static USFR | +16.7 bp/yr | +0.71 | +0.11 | 147 bp |
| Static SHV | +6.3 bp/yr | +1.40 | +0.23 | 27 bp |

333 switches over 12.4 years (**26.9 a year**); the rule sits in USFR 55.2% of days.

The gross edge is **−6.9 bp/yr at *t* = −0.29** — indistinguishable from zero and, if
anything, the wrong sign. The net loss is almost exactly what the turnover-matched random
placebo loses (−104 bp/yr on the reported seed, −88 to −121 across five, B1b), and
the *reversed* rule loses too: the switching is destroying
value through friction alone, not through a wrong-way bet. Note also the ceiling on the
whole exercise — **the best static vehicle beats BIL by 16.7 bp/yr**, while one round trip
costs 4 bps. At 27 switches a year the rule spends 108 bp chasing a 17 bp prize.

**Cost symmetry, named.** The rotation is charged on every switch; the two static arms are
charged nothing beyond the single 4 bp round trip it takes to establish them (priced
explicitly for the SGOV arm in B7), because that is what holding one fund costs. Note also
that on this window **neither static arm clears |*t*| = 2** — +16.7 at *t* = +0.71 and +6.3
at *t* = +1.40. They bound the size of the prize; they are not themselves certified edges.

### B1a. Allocation or timing? (the gross number, decomposed)

The gross rule is not a pure timing bet: it sits in USFR 55.2% of the time, and USFR and
SHV do not earn the same thing, so part of any gross number is simply *where it happened
to stand*. Splitting the two, on the same days and the same tape:

| Gross, excess of BIL | Ann. excess | HAC *t* | Bootstrap 95% CI |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Passive 55/45 USFR/SHV blend — **no trading at all** | +12.1 bp/yr | +0.91 | — |
| **The timing decision alone** (rule − that blend) | **−18.9 bp/yr** | **−0.97** | [−61.9, +18.3] |
| = the switch rule, gross | −6.9 bp/yr | −0.29 | [−55.0, +34.9] |

Neither piece clears |*t*| = 1. The small positive number in the column belongs to a
*fixed* allocation nobody had to forecast; the act of timing subtracts about 19 bp/yr and
is itself indistinguishable from zero. This is the cleanest statement of the result: the
rotation adds nothing before costs, and what little the arm earns it earns by standing
still.

### B1b. The placebo is not one lucky draw

A single random control proves nothing, so the turnover-matched placebo is re-drawn on
five seeds (net, 2 bps): −99.6, −88.1, −96.8, −121.4, −93.5 bp/yr — a range of
**[−121.4, −88.1]** that brackets the real rule's **−115.3**. The rule is an ordinary
member of the population of equally-churning coin flips.

## B2. Block-bootstrap CI on the annualised excess (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks)

| | Point | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Gross | −6.9 bp/yr | [−55.0, +34.9] | 61.1% |
| Net (2 bps) | −115.3 bp/yr | [−169.0, −67.9] | 100.0% |

The gross CI straddles zero comfortably; the net CI is entirely below it.

## B3. The whole pre-registered lookback grid (not the best of it)

Four signal windows were specified before running; all four are reported. With four
looks, a nominal |*t*| ≈ 2 on a winner would mean little — and there is no winner.

| Lookback | Gross | *t* | Net (2 bps) | *t* | Reversed (net) | Switches |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 d | −2.5 bp/yr | −0.14 | −198.2 | −9.31 | −170.8 | 604 |
| **21 d** | **−6.9** | **−0.29** | **−115.3** | **−4.39** | −78.8 | 333 |
| 63 d | +12.1 | +0.53 | −50.9 | −2.08 | −51.3 | 191 |
| 126 d | −2.6 | −0.12 | −42.0 | −1.88 | −13.1 | 117 |

The largest gross *t* anywhere in the grid is **+0.53**.

## B4. Cost sweep — the one-way cost is a PROXY/ASSUMPTION

2 bps one-way is a fair figure for a penny-wide cash ETF; it is not measured on this tape,
so it is swept. It cannot rescue the rule, because the gross edge is already zero:

| One-way cost | Excess vs BIL | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | −6.9 bp/yr | −0.29 |
| 1 bp | −61.1 | −2.45 |
| **2 bps** | **−115.3** | **−4.39** |
| 5 bps | −277.9 | −8.40 |
| 10 bps | −549.0 | −11.17 |

Even at a *zero* cost — free trading, no spread, no slippage — the rule earns nothing.

## B5. Era cut (split 2020-01-01)

| Era | n | Switch gross (*t*) | Switch net (*t*) | Static USFR (*t*) | Static SHV (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2014-2019 | 1,465 | −38.5 (−0.77) | −158.2 (−3.02) | +17.2 (+0.35) | +14.0 (**+2.25**) |
| 2020-2026 | 1,609 | +21.8 (+1.87) | −76.5 (−4.74) | +14.6 (+1.17) | −1.0 (−0.15) |

The gross edge **flips sign between eras** (−38.5 then +21.8) and clears |*t*| = 2 in
neither. SHV's own static premium over BIL is the only thing that clears the bar in either
half, and it does so in *one* half and vanishes in the other — the 2022-23 hiking cycle
punished its extra duration.

## B6. SGOV four-vehicle cross-check (2020-06-01 → 2026-06-30, n = 1,528)

| | Excess vs BIL | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| Switch rule (gross) | +11.5 bp/yr | +1.01 |
| Switch rule (net, 2 bps) | −89.5 bp/yr | −5.48 |
| **Static SGOV** | **+12.3 bp/yr** | **+3.98** |
| Static USFR | +15.7 bp/yr | +1.32 |
| Static SHV | −6.8 bp/yr | −1.21 |

## B7. The SGOV-over-BIL side finding, stress-tested

**The one robust number in the whole study is not a trade** — and it is **not the claim this
study set out to test**, so read the selection first.

> **SELECTION, named.** SGOV is the *best of the three static arms in B6*, and it was picked
> **after** seeing them. On a pure multiple-comparison view its *t* = +3.98 is one look out of
> three (plus the SHV/USFR arms in B1), so the *t* alone earns nothing. What earns it is that
> the mechanism — a published, ex-ante-knowable expense-ratio gap plus a shorter ladder — was
> *predictable before the tape was read*, and that the number survives a split-half cut. This
> is a hindsight-selected arm with an ex-ante mechanism, not a discovery.

| SGOV − BIL, daily excess | n | Excess vs BIL | HAC *t* | Bootstrap 95% CI |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Full sample** (2020-06-02 → 2026-06-30) | 1,527 | **+12.3 bp/yr** | **+3.98** | [+8.0, +16.5] |
| Early half (2020-06-02 → 2023-06-12) | 763 | +17.0 bp/yr | +3.18 | [+10.2, +23.5] |
| Late half (2023-06-13 → 2026-06-30) | 764 | +7.7 bp/yr | +1.96 | [+3.0, +12.3] |

The halves are the sample split at its own midpoint observation (no overlap). Both are
positive with a CI clear of zero, but the effect **halves** in the late period — the fee gap
narrowed as the price war did. Published expense ratios (an **ASSUMPTION** — issuer figures,
not measured here) put BIL roughly 4-5 bps above SGOV, so about a third to a half of the gap
is fee and the remainder is the shorter ladder.

**It also has to be bought once.** At the same 2 bps a leg the swap costs 4 bps as a one-off
round trip, i.e. **3.9 months of payback**, and nothing after that — against the rotation's
27 round trips a year. That asymmetry, not the *t*-stat, is the whole point.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports a real-tape stamp)

Three worlds, one detector. The panel plants a WAM ladder (the measurement effect) and a
trending rate path (the forecasting effect) **independently**, so each can be switched off.

| World | Duration spread | Switch rule, gross | *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Real ladder **+ trending rate** | +0.222 yr | **+137.8 bp/yr** | +16.02 |
| Real ladder, **unpredictable rate** (the power floor) | +0.210 yr | **+9.6 bp/yr** | **+5.30** |
| **No ladder** (the null), ×8 seeds | −0.0003 yr (sd 0.0015) | — | mean −0.77, \|*t*\|≥2 on **0/8** |

The middle row is the important one. With rate changes made *unpredictable*, the switch
rule still earns **+9.6 bp/yr at *t* = +5.30**, purely because after a run-up the short
ladder's book yield has already repriced while the long one's is stale — carry rotation,
no forecasting. That is the smallest effect this harness can see, and it sees it easily.
The real tape's duration spread (USFR → SHV = **0.178 yr**) is comparable to the planted
0.21, yet the real gross edge is **−6.9 bp/yr at *t* = −0.29** — below even the
no-forecasting floor. The harness has ample power; the tape has nothing to give it.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Mixed.** The measurement half is unambiguous and overwhelming: cash vehicles
  really do reprice with distinct, orderable lags, with realised durations of −0.001
  (USFR), +0.072 (SGOV), +0.083 (BIL) and +0.177 (SHV) years, |*t*| up to 8.1, a
  pass-through that sums to 1, a residual repricing delay of two to four weeks once
  the trailing-window artefact is stripped out, and the same ordering at |*t*| ≥ 2.8 in
  **both** eras (A4). It is also, deliberately, not a forecast: duration ≈ WAM/2 is bond
  arithmetic, so a large *t* here is a well-measured identity, not an edge. The **tradable** half is absent: the
  rate-direction switch rule earns **−6.9 bp/yr gross (HAC *t* = −0.29)** with a bootstrap
  CI [−55, +35] straddling zero, no lookback in the pre-registered grid exceeds |*t*| =
  0.53, and the gross sign flips between eras. Decomposed (B1a), the *timing* on its own
  is −18.9 bp/yr (*t* = −0.97): the rule's only positive component is the passive 55/45
  standing allocation it happens to hold, which required no forecast at all. Knowing precisely *how* each vehicle
  reprices tells you nothing about *which* to hold next month, because the trailing
  direction of ^IRX does not forecast its next move.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** The prize is bounded by the whole cross-vehicle dispersion —
  about 16 bp/yr — while a single round trip costs 4 bps and the rule trades 27 times a
  year. Net excess is −115 bp/yr at 2 bps and still −61 bp/yr at 1 bp; the
  turnover-matched placebo and the reversed rule lose the same way, which identifies the
  loss as pure friction. The only bankable finding is a **fund swap, not a trade**: hold
  SGOV rather than BIL for +12.3 bp/yr (*t* = +3.98; both halves positive, though the late
  half is only +7.7 at *t* = +1.96) and never rebalance — an arm **selected ex post** from
  B6 and defended by an ex-ante, published fee gap rather than by its *t*. It is also not
  this study's claim: the claim was the rotation, and the rotation is a mirage.
- **Risk reduction or alpha?** Neither. All four vehicles are cash; the exercise moves ~18
  bps of duration around and manufactures turnover. Even the SGOV finding is a fee-and-WAM
  identity, not a risk premium.
